snp3.9:0.2: This sutta is identical with MN 98.
snp3.9:6.2: In the Brahmanical tradition, this means the three Vedas; later in the poem the Buddha gives “three knowledges” a Buddhist redefinition.
snp3.9:8.5: Here Vāseṭṭha is referring to action in this lifetime, rather than action in previous lifetimes.
snp3.9:12.5: In this and the following verses, the Buddha plays on three meanings of the word jāti—birth, species, and nature—a point that becomes clear when he later contrasts these natural distinctions in the animal world with the merely conventional distinctions among human beings.
snp3.9:32.6: This verse begins a section whose verses are identical with Dhp 396–423, except that the last verse in this set is missing a line found at Dhp 423: “He is a sage who has mastered full-knowing, his mastery totally mastered.” The section redefines “brahman” to mean an arahant (though see the note on “the deathless,” below). As for “bho-sayer”: brahmans, when surprised or amazed, tended to use the word bho, or master, as an exclamation; “if he has anything” (reading sa ce with the Burmese and Sri Lankan editions) means if he lays claim to anything as his own.
snp3.9:34.3: The three commentaries on this verse—SnA, MA, and DhpA—treat the imagery slightly differently, though all agree that the strap stands for hatred and the thong for craving. MA simply has cord = views, bridle = view-obsession, and bar = ignorance. SnA and DhpA elaborate further: cord = the 62 wrong views listed at DN 1, and bridle = the obsessions (sensuality, becoming, anger, conceit, views, uncertainty, and ignorance; see AN 7:11–12); since ignorance is itself one of the obsessions, cutting these chariot parts automatically lifts the bar as well.
snp3.9:36.4: “With no overbearing pride”: reading anussadaṁ with the Thai, Burmese, and Sri Lankan editions. “Last-body”: since an arahant will not be reborn, this present body is his or her last.
snp3.9:38.2: Three different senses of the single word attano are at play in this verse: “for himself,” “on his own,” and “his own.”
snp3.9:47.2: According to SnA, “attachments” or “homes” (ālaya) means cravings; “knowing” here is the knowledge of full Awakening (aññā).
snp3.9:47.4: The image derives from the standard analogy of crossing a river. According to AN 7:15, gaining footing on the riverbed—before climbing up onto the bank—corresponds to the third stage of awakening, non-return; only reaching the far bank corresponds to arahantship. So this verse either uses the image differently, treating the gaining of a footing as arahantship, or else is the only verse in this set that applies “brahman” to a non-returner.
snp3.9:56.2: On the fact that even devas and brahmās cannot know the course of the arahant, see MN 49, SN 23:2, AN 11:10, and Dhp 92–93.
snp3.9:59.3: The forms of mastery listed here correspond to the three knowledges of the Buddha’s own Awakening—knowledge of previous lives, knowledge of how beings pass away and are reborn, and knowledge of the ending of the effluents (see MN 4). It’s in this verse that the Buddha redefines the “three knowledges” Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja claimed at the start, showing that their kind of knowledge doesn’t qualify one as a genuine brahman in his eyes.
snp3.9:68.1: Here the Buddha means the three knowledges as he has just redefined them, not as Vāseṭṭha originally defined them.
snp3.9:68.4: Sakka is the chief of the devas of the heaven of the Thirty-three.
